defaults.source: Standard introductory te reo Māori grammar as taught in beginner courses (e.g. the Te Whanake series). Explanations and example sentences were written by AI for this app, not copied from any course, and have not yet been reviewed by a fluent speaker.

patterns.title: te, ngā, he — the, the (plural), a
patterns.structure: te + one thing · ngā + several things · he + a / some
patterns.explanation: Most Māori nouns do not change form for the plural. The word in front shows the number: te for one thing, ngā for more than one. He means a, an or some.

patterns.title: Kei te … — happening now
patterns.structure: Kei te + action or state + who
patterns.explanation: Kei te marks something happening or true right now. The action or state comes first and the person or thing doing it comes after. The same pattern works with describing words: Kei te ngenge au (I am tired).

sentences.en: (They|They two|The two of them|Those two) are (talking|speaking).

sentences.hint: we = three or more, not including the listener

transforms.instruction: Change the subject to 'we' (three or more, not including the listener).

patterns.title: He … — describing and classifying
patterns.structure: He + what it is / what it is like + the thing
patterns.explanation: A sentence beginning with He says what something is, or what it is like. There is no word for 'is'. He kurī tēnei = This is a dog. He nui te whare = The house is big.

transforms.instruction: Change 'this' to 'that' (over there, away from both of you).

patterns.title: Ko … — identifying
patterns.structure: Ko + a specific person or thing + who / what it is
patterns.explanation: Ko introduces a specific, named person or thing. He classifies (a teacher); Ko identifies (the teacher, Mere). In these examples tōku and taku mean 'my' and tō means 'your'.

patterns.title: ki and i — adding where to and what
patterns.structure: … + ki (to, towards) + place · … + i + the thing acted on
patterns.explanation: Add detail after the subject. Ki marks a destination or direction: ki te tāone (to town). I marks the thing an action is done to: Kei te kai au i te ika (I am eating the fish). A few verbs of attention, such as titiro and whakarongo, take ki instead of i.

sentences.mi: Kei te haere au ki te tāone.
Kei te kai au i te ika.
Kei te titiro ia ki te manu.
Kei te whakarongo mātou ki te waiata.
sentences.en: We are listening to the song.
sentences.hint: we = three or more, not including the listener

sentences.mi: Kei te pānui au i te pukapuka.
Kei te horoi ia i te motokā.

transforms.from: Kei te haere au ki te tāone.
answers: Kei te haere au ki te kura.

patterns.title: I … — past
patterns.structure: I + action + who
patterns.explanation: I at the start of a sentence marks a completed action in the past. Swap Kei te for I and the rest of the sentence stays the same.

sentences.mi: I haere au ki te kura.
I kite au i te manu.
I hoko ia i te pukapuka.

sentences.hint: we = three or more, not including the listener

transforms.from: Kei te kai au i te ika.
transforms.instruction: Change to the past (I ate the fish).
answers: I kai au i te ika.

patterns.title: Ka … — future and what happens next
patterns.structure: Ka + action + who
patterns.explanation: Ka marks an action that begins or happens. On its own, or with a future time word such as āpōpō, it is usually understood as future. In storytelling it takes its time from the context.

sentences.hint: we = all of us, including the listener

sentences.mi: Ka tunu au i te kai.

transforms.from: I haere au ki te kura.
answers: Ka haere au ki te kura.

patterns.title: Kua … — has happened
patterns.structure: Kua + action + who
patterns.explanation: Kua marks something that has happened and whose result still matters now, like English 'has / have …'. Kua kai au = I have eaten.

sentences.en: The baby (has gone to sleep|has fallen asleep|is asleep).

sentences.mi: Kua pānui au i te pukapuka.

patterns.title: Questions — aha, hea, wai, pēhea
patterns.structure: Put the question word where the answer would go
patterns.explanation: A yes/no question keeps the same words as a statement and is shown by intonation or a question mark. For other questions, a question word takes the place of the answer: aha (what), hea (where), wai (who), pēhea (how).

patterns.title: Kei + place — where something is
patterns.structure: Kei + place + the thing (+ i + reference point)
patterns.explanation: Kei followed by a place says where something is now; I followed by a place says where it was. With a position word (runga, raro, roto, waho), the reference point follows i: Kei roto te ngeru i te whare. Do not confuse Kei te kura (at the school) with Kei te + action.

sentences.mi: Kei roto te ngeru i te whare.
Kei runga te pukapuka i te tēpu.
sentences.en: The book is (on|on top of) the table.

sentences.mi: Kei raro te kurī i te tēpu.

transforms.from: Kei roto te ngeru i te whare.
transforms.fromEn: The cat is inside the house.
transforms.instruction: Change the position to 'on top of'.
answers: Kei runga te ngeru i te whare.

transforms.instruction: Change to the past (were at school).

patterns.title: Kāore … — saying not
patterns.structure: Kāore + who + i te / i / e / (anō … kia) + action
patterns.explanation: To negate an action sentence, start with Kāore and move the subject in front of the verb. Kei te becomes i te; past I stays i; future Ka becomes e. Kua is negated with Kāore anō … kia (not yet).

sentences.mi: Kāore ngā tamariki i te moe.

answers: Kāore ngā tamariki i te tākaro.

patterns.title: taku, tō, tana — my, your, his/her
patterns.structure: taku / tō / tana + one thing · aku / ō / ana + several things
patterns.explanation: Taku (my), tō (your, one person) and tana (his or her) replace te before a noun. Drop the t for more than one thing: aku, ō, ana. Māori also sorts possession into two categories, a and o (tāku / tōku), depending on the relationship between owner and thing; taku and tana are neutral forms that avoid that choice. The a/o categories have their own pattern: tāku and tōku.

sentences.en: (Mere is my friend|My friend is Mere).

sentences.mi: I kite au i tō māmā.

patterns.title: Describing things — word order and tino
patterns.structure: te / he + thing + describing word · tino + describing word = very
patterns.explanation: A describing word follows the thing it describes: te whare nui (the big house). Tino in front of a describing word means very: tino pai (very good).

patterns.title: Commands — E noho! Haere mai! Kaua e …
patterns.structure: E + short verb · longer verb on its own · Kaua e + verb = don't
patterns.explanation: To tell someone to do something, use the verb on its own. Short verbs (one or two vowels long, such as noho, tū, moe, kai) take E in front: E noho! Longer verbs do not: Haere! Titiro! Mai adds 'towards me'. For 'don't', use Kaua e before any verb.

sentences.en: (Look here|Look at me|Look this way|Look over here).

transforms.instruction: Make it a negative command (don't sit).
Make it a negative command (don't come here).

patterns.title: tāku and tōku — the a and o categories, and having
patterns.structure: He + thing + tāku / tōku = I have a … · tāu / tōu (your) · tāna / tōna (his, her)
patterns.explanation: Possession is sorted into two categories. The a forms (tāku, tāu, tāna) are used for things you have control over or responsibility for: food, pets, your children, your spouse, your work, movable belongings. The o forms (tōku, tōu, tōna) are used for things you are part of or that shelter, carry or stand above you: houses, vehicles, clothing, parts of the body, feelings, names, parents, siblings and friends. He kurī tāku = I have a dog. He whare tōku = I have a house. For several things, drop the t: āku, ōku.

transforms.instruction: Change to 'You (one person) have a dog'.

transforms.explain: A vehicle carries you, so it takes the o form: tōku.

patterns.title: Me … — should, let's
patterns.structure: Me + action + who
patterns.explanation: Me before a verb makes a mild instruction or suggestion: should, had better, or (with tātou) let's. Me haere tātou = We should go / Let's go.

sentences.en: (We should go|Let us go|We had better go).
sentences.hint: we = all of us, including the listener

sentences.mi: Me whakarongo koe ki te kaiako.
sentences.en: You (should|had better) listen to the teacher.

sentences.mi: Me hoki au ki te kāinga.
sentences.en: I (should|had better) (go home|return home|go back home).

patterns.title: ki te + verb — wanting to do something
patterns.structure: Kei te pīrangi + who + ki te + action
patterns.explanation: After a verb of wanting (pīrangi, hiahia), ki te introduces the thing you want to do: Kei te pīrangi au ki te kai (I want to eat).

sentences.mi: Kei te pīrangi au ki te kai.
Kei te pīrangi ia ki te moe.
Kei te pīrangi ngā tamariki ki te tākaro.
Kei te pīrangi koe ki te haere?
Kei te hiahia au ki te ako.
Kāore au i te pīrangi ki te haere.
sentences.en: I do not want to go.

transforms.from: Kei te pīrangi au ki te kai.
answers: Kāore au i te pīrangi ki te kai.

transforms.from: Kei te pīrangi au ki te kai.
answers: Kei te pīrangi au ki te whakatā.

patterns.title: E hia? — counting things and people
patterns.structure: E + number (2–9) + ngā … · Kotahi te … · Toko- + number for people
patterns.explanation: To say how many, put the number first. Numbers two to nine take E: E rua ngā ngeru (there are two cats). One is kotahi. When counting people, two to nine take the prefix toko- instead: tokotoru ngā tamariki (three children). E hia? asks how many things; Tokohia? asks how many people.

transforms.instruction: Change 'houses' to 'teachers'. Mind how people are counted.

patterns.title: ā and i — saying when
patterns.structure: ā + time (future) · i + time (past)
patterns.explanation: A time phrase usually goes at the end. Use ā before a time that is still to come and i before a time that has passed: ā te Rāhina (on Monday, coming), i te Rāhina (on Monday, gone). Tērā wiki means that week: ā tērā wiki is next week, i tērā wiki is last week.

sentences.mi: Ka haere au ā te Rāhina.
I mahi au i te Rātū.
Ka hoki mai rātou ā tērā wiki.
I tae mai ia i tērā wiki.
Ka tīmata te hui ā te Rāmere.

transforms.from: Ka haere au ā te Rāhina.
transforms.instruction: Change to the past (I went on Monday).
answers: I haere au i te Rāhina.

patterns.title: Nō hea koe? — where someone is from
patterns.structure: Nō + place + who
patterns.explanation: Nō means from or belonging to. Nō hea koe? asks where you are from, and the answer puts the place where hea was: Nō Ōtautahi au.

sentences.hint: we = three or more, not including the listener

transforms.instruction: Ask the same of two people.

patterns.title: ēnei, ēnā, ērā and nei, nā, rā — these and those
patterns.structure: ēnei / ēnā / ērā + things · te … nei / nā / rā
patterns.explanation: Tēnei, tēnā and tērā drop the t for more than one thing: ēnei (these), ēnā (those near you), ērā (those over there). The same three positions can follow the noun as nei, nā and rā: te kurī nei (this dog), te whare rā (that house over there).

patterns.title: Kia … — be …, and good wishes
patterns.structure: Kia + describing word
patterns.explanation: Kia before a describing word tells or wishes someone to be that way: Kia kaha! (Be strong.) It also makes wishes: Kia pai tō rā (Have a good day).

patterns.title: E … ana — in progress
patterns.structure: E + action + ana + who
patterns.explanation: E … ana wraps around a verb to show an action in progress. Unlike Kei te, it does not fix the time: context decides whether it is, was or will be happening. In everyday speech it is often used just like Kei te.

sentences.hint: they = three or more; use e … ana

transforms.instruction: Say the same using e … ana.
Say the same using e … ana.

patterns.title: a — before names and pronouns
patterns.structure: ki a / i a + name or pronoun
patterns.explanation: After ki, i, kei and similar small words, a person's name or a pronoun takes a in front: ki a Mere (to Mere), i a ia (him or her). The exception is au when written as ahau, where the a is already built in: ki ahau.

sentences.mi: Kei te kōrero au ki a Mere.
I kite au i a ia.
Kei te tatari mātou ki a koe.
sentences.hint: we = three or more, not including the listener; you = one person

sentences.mi: Kei te āwhina ia i a Hēmi.
I whakarongo ngā tamariki ki a rātou.

transforms.from: I kite au i te kurī.
answers: I kite au i a Mere.

transforms.from: Kei te kōrero au ki te kaiako.
transforms.fromEn: I am talking to the teacher.
answers: Kei te kōrero au ki a ia.

patterns.title: He pai ki a au … — liking
patterns.structure: He pai ki a + who + the thing liked
patterns.explanation: To say you like something, say it is good to you: He pai ki a au te kawhe (I like coffee). The person who likes it follows ki a; the thing liked comes last.

sentences.mi: He pai ki a au te kawhe.
He pai ki a ia te waiata.
He pai ki a koe te tiakarete?
He pai ki ngā tamariki te tākaro.
He tino pai ki a au te kai moana.

transforms.from: He pai ki a au te kawhe.
answers: He pai ki a ia te kawhe.

transforms.from: He pai ki a au te kawhe.
answers: He pai ki a au te tī.

patterns.title: Ehara … i te … — is not a …
patterns.structure: Ehara + thing + i te + what it is not
patterns.explanation: Sentences that say what something is (He … and Ko …) are not negated with Kāore. Use Ehara, then the subject, then i te: He kurī tēnei becomes Ehara tēnei i te kurī (This is not a dog).

sentences.mi: Ehara tērā i te whare hou.
sentences.en: That is not a new house.

patterns.title: Kāore … i + place — not there
patterns.structure: Kāore + the thing + i + place
patterns.explanation: To say something is not somewhere, start with Kāore, then the subject, and change Kei to i: Kei te kura ngā tamariki becomes Kāore ngā tamariki i te kura.

sentences.mi: Kāore ngā tamariki i te kura.
Kāore te ngeru i roto i te whare.
sentences.en: The cat is not (inside|in) the house.

sentences.mi: Kāore te pukapuka i runga i te tēpu.
sentences.en: The book is not (on|on top of) the table.

answers: Kāore ngā tamariki i te kura.

patterns.title: Kei a … — who has it
patterns.structure: Kei a + person + the thing
patterns.explanation: To say who has something with them right now, say the thing is 'at' that person: Kei a au te pukapuka (I have the book). This is about who is holding it, not who owns it. Use I a for the past.

sentences.mi: I a ia te pēke inanahi.

patterns.title: Nō … / Nā … — belongs to
patterns.structure: Nō / Nā + owner + the thing
patterns.explanation: To say who something belongs to, start with Nō (o category) or Nā (a category), then the owner. With pronouns these join up: nōku / nāku (mine), nōu / nāu (yours), nōna / nāna (his, hers). Nō wai? and Nā wai? ask whose.

transforms.instruction: Change 'the house' to 'the dog'. Mind the category.
transforms.explain: A pet is something you have responsibility for, so it takes the a form: nā.

patterns.title: tō mātou, tā rāua — our, their
patterns.structure: tā / tō + pronoun + one thing · ā / ō + pronoun + several things
patterns.explanation: With pronouns for two or more people, the possessive is two words: tā or tō (a or o category) followed by the pronoun. Tō mātou whare = our house. Drop the t for several things: ō tātou hoa = our friends.

sentences.hint: our = three or more, not including the listener
our = all of us, including the listener

transforms.instruction: Change to 'their house' (three or more people).

patterns.title: ake and iho — more and less
patterns.structure: He + describing word + ake + thing + i + what it is compared with
patterns.explanation: Ake after a describing word means more; i introduces what it is compared with: He nui ake te maunga i te puke (The mountain is bigger than the hill). Iho is used the same way for less or lower.

sentences.mi: He nui ake te maunga i te puke.
sentences.en: The mountain is (bigger|larger) than the hill.

sentences.mi: He pai ake tēnei i tēnā.
He tere ake te motokā i te pahikara.
He iti iho te ngeru i te kurī.
sentences.en: The cat is smaller than the dog.

sentences.mi: He roa ake te awa i te huarahi.
sentences.en: The river is longer than the road.

transforms.instruction: Say it is bigger than the hill.
answers: He nui ake te maunga i te puke.

patterns.title: tonu, kē, anō — still, already, again
patterns.structure: action + tonu / kē / anō
patterns.explanation: Small words placed straight after the verb add meaning. Tonu: still, continuing. Kē: already, or contrary to what was expected. Anō: again.

sentences.mi: Kei te ako tonu au i te reo Māori.
sentences.en: I am still learning (the Māori language|Māori|te reo Māori).
(Say it again|Say that again|Tell me again).

patterns.title: ki te + verb — in order to
patterns.structure: … + ki te + action
patterns.explanation: Ki te before a verb can give the purpose of going somewhere or doing something: I haere au ki te toa ki te hoko kai (I went to the shop to buy food).

sentences.mi: I haere au ki te toa ki te hoko kai.
sentences.en: I went to the (shop|store) to buy food.

sentences.mi: Kei te haere ia ki te whare pukapuka ki te pānui.
sentences.en: (She|He) is going to the library to read.

sentences.mi: I hoki mai rātou ki te kai.
Ka haere au ki te tāone ki te mahi.
sentences.en: I will go to (town|the town) to work.

transforms.from: I haere au ki te toa.
transforms.instruction: Add the purpose: to buy food.
answers: I haere au ki te toa ki te hoko kai.

patterns.title: nā te mea — because
patterns.structure: statement + nā te mea + reason
patterns.explanation: Nā te mea joins a statement to its reason. What follows is an ordinary sentence: Kei te ngenge au nā te mea i mahi au (I am tired because I worked).

sentences.mi: Kei te ngenge au nā te mea i mahi au.
sentences.en: I am tired because I worked.

sentences.mi: Kāore au i haere nā te mea i māuiui au.
sentences.en: I did not go because I was (sick|unwell|ill).

sentences.mi: Kei te harikoa ia nā te mea kua tae mai tōna māmā.
Kei te noho au ki te kāinga nā te mea kei te ua.
sentences.en: I am staying (home|at home) because it is raining.

transforms.instruction: Add the reason: because I worked.
answers: Kei te ngenge au nā te mea i mahi au.

patterns.title: Ki te … ka … — if
patterns.structure: Ki te + action + who, ka + result
patterns.explanation: Ki te at the start of a sentence, before a verb, means if, for something that may happen. The result follows with ka: Ki te ua, ka noho au ki te kāinga (If it rains, I will stay home).

sentences.mi: Ki te ua, ka noho au ki te kāinga.
sentences.en: If it rains, I will stay (home|at home).

sentences.mi: Ki te haere koe, ka haere au.
sentences.en: If you go, I will go.

sentences.mi: Ki te pai te rangi, ka haere tātou ki tātahi.
sentences.en: If the weather is (fine|good), we will go to the beach.
sentences.hint: we = all of us, including the listener

sentences.mi: Ki te ngenge koe, me whakatā.
sentences.en: If you are tired, (you should rest|rest|you had better rest).

transforms.from: Ka noho au ki te kāinga.
transforms.instruction: Add the condition: if it rains.
answers: Ki te ua, ka noho au ki te kāinga.

patterns.title: E hia ō tau? — age
patterns.structure: number + ōku / ōu / ōna + tau
patterns.explanation: Age is stated as the number of years you have: Tekau ōku tau (I am ten; literally, my years are ten). Numbers two to nine take E. E hia ō tau? asks how old you are.

sentences.mi: E whitu ngā tau o taku tamāhine.
E hia ngā tau o tō kurī?

patterns.title: Passive — I kainga te ika e te ngeru
patterns.structure: tense marker + verb with passive ending + thing acted on (+ e + doer)
patterns.explanation: The passive is very common in Māori. The verb takes an ending (often -a, -ia, -tia, -na, -ngia; each verb has its usual one), the thing acted on becomes the subject with no i in front, and the doer, if mentioned, follows e. I kai te ngeru i te ika becomes I kainga te ika e te ngeru (The fish was eaten by the cat). Endings used here: kai → kainga, tuhi → tuhia, horoi → horoia, hoko → hokona, kite → kitea, tunu → tunua. Note that kainga (eaten) has no macron; kāinga is home.

sentences.mi: I kainga te ika e te ngeru.
sentences.en: The fish was eaten by the cat.

sentences.mi: I tuhia te reta e Mere.
sentences.en: The letter was written by Mere.

sentences.mi: Ka tunua te kai e Hēmi.
sentences.en: The food will be cooked by Hēmi.

transforms.from: I kai te ngeru i te ika.
transforms.instruction: Make it passive (The fish was eaten by the cat).
answers: I kainga te ika e te ngeru.

transforms.from: I tuhi a Mere i te reta.
transforms.instruction: Make it passive (The letter was written by Mere).
answers: I tuhia te reta e Mere.

patterns.title: Nā … i … / Mā … e … — who did it, who will do it
patterns.structure: Nā + doer + thing + i + verb (past) · Mā + doer + thing + e + verb (future)
patterns.explanation: To stress who did something, start with Nā and the doer, then the thing, then i and the verb: Nā Mere te kai i tunu (It was Mere who cooked the food). For the future, use Mā … e …: Māku ngā pereti e horoi (I will be the one to wash the plates). There is no i before the thing acted on. With pronouns: nāku, nāu, nāna; māku, māu, māna.

sentences.mi: Nā Mere te kai i tunu.
sentences.en: (Mere cooked the food|It was Mere who cooked the food).
(I wrote the letter|It was I who wrote the letter|It was me who wrote the letter).
(I will wash the plates|I will be the one to wash the plates).

sentences.mi: Mā wai te kai e tunu?

transforms.from: Nā Mere te kai i tunu.
transforms.instruction: Change to the future (Mere will cook the food).
answers: Mā Mere te kai e tunu.
Nā wai te reta i tuhi?

patterns.title: Ka taea e au … — can
patterns.structure: Ka taea e + who + te + action
patterns.explanation: Taea means to be achievable. To say someone can do something, say it can be achieved by them: Ka taea e au te kaukau (I can swim). The doer follows e, and the action follows te. Negative: Kāore e taea e au … (I cannot …).

sentences.mi: Ka taea e au te kaukau.
Ka taea e ia te waiata.
Ka taea e koe te taraiwa?
Kāore e taea e au te haere.
Ka taea e ngā tamariki te pānui.

transforms.from: Ka taea e au te kaukau.
answers: Kāore e taea e au te kaukau.

transforms.from: Ka taea e au te kaukau.
answers: Ka taea e ia te kaukau.
